# The Institute of Possible Weather

The Institute occupied the basement of a municipal observatory that had been obsolete for sixty-three years. Its telescopes pointed at nothing but pigeon nests and weather stains, but beneath them, behind a steel door marked ATMOSPHERIC RESEARCH, the Institute maintained its own climate.

Mara Venn had worked there for eleven years.

Her title was archivist of unrealized conditions. Her job was to catalogue weather that had never happened: rain that fell upward, snow in the shape of handwritten apologies, fog that preserved the scent of lilacs for exactly one evening.

The Institute’s collection contained four thousand three hundred and twelve storms in glass jars.

Some were theatrical. Thunder that rolled across ceilings without entering rooms. A cyclone confined to a thimble. Hailstones the size of diamonds that shattered into moths.

Others were modest. A shower limited to a single balcony. Dew on windows through which no one had looked. The particular warmth of a September afternoon remembered by almost everyone and occurring to almost no one.

Mara liked the modest ones best.

She worked in a long room lit by green lamps. Shelves rose toward the ceiling, their jars clouded with age, sealed with wax, labelled in six languages. The air smelled faintly of dust, iron, and petrichor, although no one was certain why petrichor appeared in an underground room. The Institute’s founders had explained that it came from “atmospheric longing,” a phrase Mara had once dismissed as nonsense and had since come to regard as a unit of measurement.

Each jar had a card.

The cards recorded the weather’s essential qualities, its impossible feature, and the precise circumstances under which it might have been expected.

JAR 2917: RAIN OF SMALL UNFINISHED SONGS.

Colour: pewter.

Duration: until the singer remembers the second verse.

Impossible feature: rain audible only to those who have withheld an apology.

Status: unrealized.

There were other statuses, though the older ones had been discontinued.

Partially realized. Temporarily forgotten. Too dangerous. Disbelieved.

The newest cards used a simpler language: possible, probable, pending.

Mara’s rule was written at the top of her desk in blue ink:

A weather is not true because we remember it.  
A weather is not false because we have forgotten it.  
A memory is not weather unless it carries weight.

Director Solven arrived at nine, as he did every morning, carrying a clean handkerchief and a stain of optimism on his cuff.

“The grant committee meets Friday,” he said.

“I know.”

“We need twelve exceptional specimens.”

“We have four thousand three hundred and twelve.”

“Not specimens. Exceptions.” He set a folder on her desk. “The committee has requested weather capable of changing civilization.”

Mara looked at him.

“Can weather do that?”

“Weather has altered wars, harvests, elections. It has inspired music, produced religious conversions, and toppled governments indirectly through crop failure.”

“Indirectly through crop failure,” Mara repeated.

“Don’t be defeatist. The committee is looking for wonder.”

“We are an archive.”

“An archive is a library whose books have never been opened. There is a difference.” He tapped the folder. “They want storms with historical significance.”

“Jar two hundred and eight is a fog that makes everyone speak in their native language after thirty years of pretending not to know it.”

Solven glanced at it.

“It sounds embarrassing.”

“It is historically significant.”

“It is not exceptional.”

Mara returned to her card.

Solven remained a moment, watching the green light move across the glass shelves. His reflection appeared in hundreds of jars, broken into small, slightly worried men.

“The future section opens next month,” he said.

“Next month?”

“Probable weather. Conditions likely to occur within the century.”

“That isn’t possible.”

“That is why we are discussing it.”

He left with his optimism neatly folded into the folder under his arm.

Mara drew a fresh card and wrote the date. Then she wrote the atmospheric pressure, which was normal, and the humidity, which was normal, and the wind, which was absent. The jar before her was unremarkable except that it had no number.

She had found it on the lower shelf during the previous night’s inventory, behind a box of lightning that smelled faintly of burned hair. It was small and squat, shaped like a pudding bowl. Its lid was sealed with grey wax. There was condensation beneath the glass.

Rain, Mara thought.

Not the Institute’s usual impossible varieties. Just rain.

She held the jar to the lamp. Inside, drops moved against its sides. They fell upward, paused, then descended in no recognizable pattern. A pale light flickered within it, though no storm was visible.

The smell reached her before she could identify it.

Warm stone. Bicycle bells. Cut grass. Orange peel.

Someone’s street on a summer afternoon.

Mara placed the jar on her desk and opened the catalogue drawer marked INADMISSIBLE. The drawer resisted, as they always did. Inside were cards for things the Institute could not classify: weather dependent upon a person’s name, storms occurring only in translations, a heat that burned wherever the speaker had been dishonest.

The first rule prevented that classification.

A weather is not weather unless it can occur without its witness.

Mara copied the sentence onto a new card. She wrote:

JAR: UNNUMBERED.

COLOUR: unclassified.

DURATION: uncertain.

IMPOSSIBLE FEATURE: rain on an unnamed street.

STATUS: unrecorded.

Then she added a note she had never added before.

Smell: orange peel, bells, rain on warm pavement.

Solven appeared behind her.

“Where did that come from?”

“The lower shelf.”

“There is no lower shelf. There is the lower collection.”

“It was behind the lightning.”

“Those have been sealed since the reorganization.”

“Perhaps someone forgot.”

Solven reached for the jar. Mara moved it away.

His hand stopped in the air.

“You are being proprietary,” he said.

“It is unrecorded.”

“Everything is unrecorded until we determine whether it matters.”

“That isn’t the rule.”

“No. It is a better rule.”

He straightened his cuffs. “The committee does not want ordinary rain.”

“Most rain is ordinary.”

“Most rain is not remarkable.”

“Most rain is not remarkable,” Mara agreed, “but it is still rain.”

Solven gave her a long, tired look. He had the expression of a man who had spent his life preparing exceptional dinners for people who wanted only salt.

“Find it a history,” he said. “A cyclone, a revolution, a king’s death. Otherwise we cannot save it.”

Mara did not answer.

The jar made a small sound inside her desk.

A bell.

Then another, several streets away.

Then a third, very close.

Mara remembered riding through the neighborhood on her mother’s bicycle. She had been ten, or eleven, or some age that refused to become fixed. The bicycle had a blue basket and a bell shaped like a silver pear. On wet days the bell sounded twice as loud. Her mother pedaled slowly, even when the road was clear.

What had her mother been thinking?

That was the trouble with old streets. They opened doors one had believed permanently locked. They returned smells without warning. They offered the mind a former self and asked it to compare her with the person who had stood there.

Mara put the jar in her coat pocket.

The afternoon passed without incident. She catalogued a weather of falling shadows, a mist that made everyone see themselves as they would appear in ten years, and a sunlit shower that lasted exactly as long as a goodbye. She completed the paperwork. She replaced the green lamp. She listened to the building settle around her, its pipes making sounds like distant applause.

At five o'clock, she left.

The city was dry.

Heat shimmered above the pavement. Traffic lights changed with enormous indifference. People stood beneath awnings and complained about the weather, though they had not yet been rained upon.

Mara walked toward the river.

She had taken the wrong turning.

The street was unfamiliar only in its details. A shop sold tea, a laundrette displayed three identical shirts, and outside a bakery a boy was reading a book upside down. Nothing looked impossible. That was the cruelty of places that might have belonged to another life: they did not announce themselves. They waited to be recognized.

She heard bicycle bells behind her.

They came closer, then stopped.

When Mara turned, no bicycle was there. Only a parked car, its windows reflecting a row of narrow houses. In the reflection, a woman stood beneath a tree, holding a bicycle basket full of green apples.

Mara kept walking.

The jar grew heavier.

She could feel rain inside it, moving against the fabric of her coat. A coldness seeped through the lining, followed by a sweetness that reminded her of something she had never smelled but somehow recognized.

Orange peel. Warm pavement. A bicycle bell ringing twice.

She passed a bridge, a school, a boarded-up theatre. She had lived in the city all her life, but these streets seemed to be arranging themselves around an absence. A gap in the pavement. An empty balcony. A window through which someone was watching her pass.

At the river, she found the Institute’s old courtyard.

It was officially a storage area, used for ladders, broken chairs, and instruments too obsolete even for the observatory. The courtyard was surrounded by high walls and paved with cracked stone. Three plane trees grew from the cracks, their leaves making a dry, confidential sound.

Mara placed the jar on the ground.

The wax seal had softened.

She cut it with the tip of her pen.

The first drop fell upward.

It rose above the jar, hung in the air, and came down again upon her hand. It was warm. Not the warmth of blood, but the warmth of a stone wall after summer rain.

The second drop fell into the jar.

The third fell onto the pavement.

A small dark circle appeared beneath it.

Then another. Another.

Rain began inside the courtyard, but only in one area, no larger than a rug. It stopped at the edge of the paving stones, as if the weather had been poured from a pitcher and the pitcher had been set down too quickly.

The rain smelled of bicycle bells.

Mara stepped into it.

Her shoes darkened. Her hair loosened at the temples. Water touched her face with the delicate insistence of a memory trying to return.

“Hello,” someone said.

She turned.

The courtyard was empty.

The voice came again.

“Hello.”

It belonged to an old woman standing beneath the far wall. Mara had not seen her enter. The woman wore a blue coat and held a shopping bag against her stomach.

“Can you hear it?” Mara asked.

The old woman tilted her head.

“The rain?”

“Yes.”

“I hear bells.”

The drops struck the pavement in a pattern. Not randomly. Three short, two long, three short.

The woman’s expression changed.

“My husband used to ring his bicycle bell like that,” she said. “Every evening. I would know it anywhere.”

“Where did he ride?”

“Along the canal.”

Mara knew, without knowing how she knew, that the canal path had been rebuilt.

“Was he a courier?”

“Once.”

“What color was the bicycle?”

The old woman closed her eyes.

“Red.”

Inside the jar, something struck the glass.

The rain intensified. It rose from the paving stones in silver threads. The courtyard filled with the smell of wet earth, although the earth was dry beneath the stones. Somewhere beyond the walls, a car alarm began to sound, then stopped.

The old woman opened her eyes.

“He would bring me lilacs,” she said. “In winter, sometimes. I told him they wouldn’t grow. He said that wasn’t the point.”

The rain was only around Mara now. The old woman stood several paces away, untouched.

“Why did you bring it here?” she asked.

Mara looked at the jar.

“I didn’t know it was real.”

“It isn’t real.”

“That isn’t always the same thing.”

Solven entered the courtyard carrying a black case of instruments. He stopped when he saw the rain.

His eyes narrowed with professional interest.

“Localized precipitation,” he said. “Radius approximately two meters. No visible cloud formation. Temperature differential negligible.”

He opened the case and removed a silver rod, a compass, and three small glass discs.

The compass needle spun.

The first disc clouded.

The second cracked.

The third displayed a symbol Mara did not recognize.

Solven studied the symbol.

“Interesting.”

“Is it?”

“Impossible.”

“That isn’t the same as uninteresting.”

The old woman had not moved. Solven had not noticed her.

“The rain is responding to memory,” Mara said.

“Memories do not produce precipitation.”

“Not usually.”

He glanced at her sharply.

Mara touched the surface of the jar. A drop struck her finger and broke into smaller drops. For an instant she heard her mother laughing. It was not the laugh Mara remembered from childhood. It was a laugh from a day that had not happened, or had happened elsewhere, or had been waiting patiently for her to make enough room for it.

“What is the objective event?” Solven demanded.

“An afternoon.”

“An afternoon is not an event.”

“It can be.”

“It is a duration.”

“It can be more than that.”

Solven looked toward the courtyard wall.

Then he looked again.

“Who is standing there?”

The old woman lifted one hand.

Solven took out a notebook.

“Name?”

“Elianor Voss.”

“Address?”

“You wouldn’t know it.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s the answer I have.”

He wrote something down.

The rain began to fade.

It sank into the stones, leaving a dark oval beneath Mara’s feet. The smell of bicycle bells grew fainter. The orange peel disappeared. The last drop fell from the jar and landed on its rim, trembling.

Mara closed the lid.

Silence returned to the courtyard.

Solven checked his instruments.

“Residual moisture,” he said. “Unusual mineral composition. No identifiable source.”

The old woman walked toward the gate. On the wall behind her, a bicycle leaned beneath a window that had not been there when Mara entered. It was red.

The woman paused.

“Send it back,” she said, without turning around.

“To whom?”

“Whoever keeps the other afternoons.”

Then she left.

Solven watched her go.

“Possibility,” he said, “is not sufficient.”

Mara picked up the jar.

“No,” she replied. “But it is more than we had.”

That evening, she did not catalogue the weather.

For the first time in eleven years, she left a card blank.

The next morning, a jar appeared on her desk. It contained a small storm with a perfectly circular center, and on its side, written in condensation, were the words:

DID YOU EVER WISH YOU HAD TAKEN THE OTHER ROAD?

Mara read the question twice.

Then she found a pen.

“Frequently,” she wrote.

Outside, the weather remained clear. Above the city, the obsolete telescopes pointed toward the pigeons and the untroubled blue. But in the basement of the old observatory, four thousand three hundred and twelve impossible mornings waited in their jars, and one by one, in the stillness between one minute and the next, they began to listen.
